implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy implements the strategy natively: every class gets a table, each subclass table takes ForeignKey('employee.id') as its primary key, and the base declares __mapper_args__ = {'polymorphic_on': 'type', 'polymorphic_identity': 'employee'} while each subclass sets its own polymorphic_identity. What replaces the classic mapper is the declarative mapping plus the identity map - querying the base returns Engineer and Manager instances and SQLAlchemy renders the JOIN along the path. Note the documented limit: only one discriminator column is supported for the whole hierarchy, so a second level of subclasses reuses the base column rather than introducing a new one; a hand-written mapper is justified only when the unit of work fights a fixed schema.
pitfalls: Only one discriminator column may be configured for the entire hierarchy - cascading identities on deeper subclasses are not supported, so a second level must live in the same column.
The subclass primary key must carry the foreign key; a separately generated surrogate key loses the one-to-one guarantee, and polymorphic loads join on the wrong column.
